message.content:
**PaperTrail (2026)** extracts claims and evidence from scholarly papers offline, storing them in a JSON knowledge base with associated **citations**, **section names**, and evidence snippets to anchor provenance at claim granularity, enabling real-time matching to LLM answers without relying on query-based retrieval.[2]

**Citation-anchored extraction** formalizes attribution by mapping statements to cited passages, evaluating via citation coverage (recall) and sufficiency (precision); PaperTrail refines this by decomposing papers and answers into discrete claims for finer alignment, contrasting coarser RAG passage retrieval.[2]

**Span prediction with LLMs** appears in PaperTrail's model-agnostic pipeline: offline paper-level extraction preprocesses entire corpora into claim-evidence units (potentially including spans via sections), while real-time answer extraction decomposes LLM outputs for similarity-based matching using SPECTER embeddings on scientific text; exact **page/paragraph/line** anchoring (e.g., **Bekker** or **Stephanus**) is not explicitly detailed, though section names and evidence snippets imply span-level grounding.[2]

**Verification pipelines** in PaperTrail use a three-stage process—offline paper extraction, real-time answer extraction, and claim-evidence matching—to expose **omissions**, **mismatches**, and grounding, verifying if answer claims align with source claims rather than entire passages; this differs from baseline citation interfaces that show verbatim source text without decomposition.[2]

**Pitfalls** like **citation drift** (where citations become imprecise over time) and **hallucinated Bekker numbers** are unaddressed in available 2024-2026 literature; evidence on anchoring to exact spans (e.g., **page**, **paragraph**, **Bekker**, **Stephanus**, **line**) in philosophy/classical texts is thin, with PaperTrail focusing on modern scholarly articles via sections rather than pagination systems.[2]

No primary ACL/EMNLP/NAACL/TACL/CoNLL/arXiv sources beyond PaperTrail (arXiv 2026) directly cover these; related works like Li et al. (2023) and Pang et al. (2025) inform sourcing but lack span specifics.[2]
